answer.rationale: p99 write-path latency began climbing 90 minutes ago, roughly 30 minutes after a release shipped — temporal correlation points at the new build as the most likely cause. memory_b1 supports rollback as a fast, customer-safe recovery when a release correlates with an error/latency spike, and I verified it against the archive before committing. memory_b3 argues for capacity ahead of peaks, but settlement traffic is at its normal daily peak (not an anomalous surge), so provisioning headroom treats the symptom while the suspect build keeps degrading the write path; it can follow in the next window if rollback doesn't restore latency. Failover, circuit breakers, and read-replica routing don't match the failure signature (write-path, single-region, post-release). Rollback is reversible and preserves in-flight writes; the residual risk is that the release is innocent and the peak load is the true cause, which is why post-rollback latency is the checkpoint before any further action.
